scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Here’s a quick “Diwali‑prep” playbook that keeps the most important things front‑and‑center while still letting you finish the fun bits on time. | Priority | Why it matters | What to do | Time‑frame (if you’re working from today) | |----------|----------------|------------|-------------------------------------------| | **1. Safety first** | Diyas, candles, and electric lights can be fire hazards if not handled properly. | • Check all electrical outlets, extension cords, and wiring for damage.
• Keep diyas away from curtains, paper, and anything flammable.
• If you’re using real candles, consider LED “diyas” or a fire‑proof diyas holder.
• Have a fire extinguisher or a bucket of water handy. | **Day 1** (today) – 30 min | | **2. Clean & declutter** | A tidy home feels more festive and reduces the chance of accidents. | • Sweep/vacuum floors, wipe surfaces, and clean windows.
• Put away clutter, especially in high‑traffic areas. | **Day 1** – 1 hr | | **3. Diyas & lighting** | Diyas are the heart of Diwali décor and set the mood. | • Decide on the type (real, LED, or electric).
• Arrange them in a safe, visible spot (e.g., a small table, a window sill, or a decorative diyas stand).
• If you’re using real candles, light them just before guests arrive. | **Day 2** – 30 min | | **4. Decorative accents** | Garlands, rangoli, and flowers add color and tradition. | • Hang garlands (electric or paper) around doors, windows, and the living‑room.
• Create a simple rangoli in the entryway or on the floor.
• Place fresh flowers or a small floral arrangement in a vase. | **Day 3** – 1 hr | | **5. Food & refreshments** | Food is a big part of the celebration, and you’ll want to be ready to serve. | • Plan a simple menu (snacks, sweets, a main dish).
• Prep ingredients that can be made ahead (e.g., sweets, chutneys).
• Set up a serving area with plates, napkins, and utensils. | **Day 4** – 2 hrs (prep) | | **6. Final touches & guest‑ready** | A polished finish shows you’ve put thought into the celebration. | • Light the diyas (or switch on LED lights) just before guests arrive.
• Put out a welcome mat or a small “welcome” sign.
• Do a quick walk‑through to make sure everything feels balanced. | **Day 5** – 30 min | ### Quick “Diwali‑prep” Checklist (for the next 5 days) 1. **Day 1** – Safety checks + deep clean. 2. **Day 2** – Set up diyas, test lights. 3. **Day 3** – Hang garlands, do rangoli, add flowers. 4. **Day 4** – Prep food, set up serving area. 5. **Day 5** – Final walk‑through, light diyas, welcome guests. --- #### Pro Tips - **Use LED diyas** if you’re worried about open flames. They’re safe, long‑lasting, and still look authentic. - **Create a “Diwali station”**: a small table with a candle, a small bowl of sweets, and a welcome note. - **Ask for help**: If you have family or friends who can help with a quick clean‑up or setting up decorations, it’ll free up your time for the more personal touches. - **Keep a “panic kit”**: a fire extinguisher, a bucket of water, and a spare set of lights in case something goes wrong. --- **Bottom line:** Start with safety and cleaning, then set up the diyas, finish the décor, and finish with food. That way you’ll have a warm, safe, and festive home ready for your relatives to enjoy. Happy Diwali! 🌟
